courses.subject: UGFN
courses.title: In Dialogue with Nature
courses.description:
This course invites students to engage in the intellectual pursuit of understanding humanity through the study of nature. Students will examine fundamental and enduring issues arising from human interactions with the natural world, including how humans approach nature, the knowledge developed to understand nature, and how such understanding affects and is influenced by values. From antiquity to modern times, a range of reasoned approaches have been employed to address these issues. This human enquiry leads to a reflection on the human understanding of nature and humans’ place in nature.

From selected classical writings of great thinkers who have tackled fundamental and enduring issues, students will gain a general understanding of the concepts and methodologies of science, and of how scientists relate their academic pursuits to contemporary life. Students will read, discuss and write about a selected range of texts covering major scientific discoveries, scientific methodology, philosophy, and history of science. Emphasis will be placed on students’ ability to respond critically to these texts and relate them to timeless human questions and contemporary world issues. Through these learning activities, students are expected to develop a lifelong capacity and enthusiasm to engage with texts as a living vehicle for participating in enduring dialogues on nature, science, and humanity.

courses.required_readings:
The teacher will select six texts from the eight texts included in *In Dialogue with Nature: Textbook for General Education Foundation Programme*, 3rd ed.:

* Darwin, Charles. *On the Origin of Species*, 1st ed.
[Selection: Chapter 4 (Para. 1-6, 9-18, 39-46, 50-63, 68-71)]
* Kandel, Eric R. *In Search of Memory: The Emergence of a New Science of Mind*. New York: W. W. Norton & Company, 2006.
[Selection: Chapter 4 (Para. 1-9), Chapter 28 (whole)]
* Leopold, Aldo. *A Sand County Almanac and Sketches Here and There*. New York: Oxford University Press, 2020.
[Selection: Foreword (pp. xxi-xxiii). Part I: February–Good Oak (pp. 6-16). Part II: Arizona and New Mexico–Thinking Like a Mountain (pp. 120-123). Part III: The Upshot–The Land Ethic (pp. 190-212).]
* Newton, Isaac. *The Principia: Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy*. Trans. I. Bernard Cohen and Anne Whitman. Berkeley: University of California Press, 1999.
[Selection: Author’s Preface to the Reader (pp. 381-383). Definitions: Definitions 1-5 (pp.403-406), last paragraph of Definition 6 (p. 408). Axioms, or the Laws of Motion: Laws 1-3 (pp. 416-417), Corollary 6 with Proposition 1 (pp. 443-445). Book 3: Rules for the Study of Natural Philosophy (pp.794-796). General Scholium (pp.939-944).]
* Plato. *Republic*. Trans. C.D.C. Reeve. Indianapolis: Hackett Publishing, 2004.
[Selection: 506d (Book VI) to 517e (Book VII)]
* Poincaré, Henri. *Science and Method*. Rpt. In *The Value of Science: Essential Writings of Henri Poincaré*. New York: Modern Library, 2001.
[Selection: Chapters I and III]
* Ronan, Colin A and Joseph Needham. *The Shorter Science and Civilisation in China: An Abridgement of Joseph Needham’s Original Text*. Vol. 1. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1978.
[Selection: Chapter 10 (Para. 1-3, 13-42)]
* Watson, James D. with Andrew Berry. *DNA: The Secret of Life*. New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 2003.
[Selection: Chapter 1 (Para. 1-36), Chapter 2 (whole)]
